descs.t: The Federal Reserve kept interest rates unchanged at its October meeting even with inflation still elevated. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh also announced plans to change the Fed's meeting schedule starting in fall 2027. We walk through what was decided and what Warsh said.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh held interest rates steady despite elevated inflation, and paired the pause with a plan to remove one of the Fed's rate setting votes beginning in fall 2027. We look at why the Fed chose to wait and what fewer policy meetings could mean for markets and borrowers.

Inflation is still elevated and the Federal Reserve chose to do nothing on rates, while Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced an overhaul of how often the Fed sets them. We break down who gains, who pays, and what this shift says about where the Fed is heading under Warsh.

intro.plain: The Federal Reserve just kept interest rates unchanged, even with inflation still elevated. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh also announced a plan to change the Fed's meeting schedule starting in fall 2027. That matters for mortgages, car loans and savings. So chat, are you feeling prices go up where you live, or has it settled down?
intro.mid: The Fed held rates again, and inflation is still high. Kevin Warsh did not stop there: he wants to eliminate one of the Fed's rate setting votes starting in fall 2027. Fewer meetings means bigger moments when they do act. So tell me in the chat: is the Fed being careful here, or falling behind?
intro.bold: Inflation is still elevated and the Fed just decided to wait. At the same time Chair Kevin Warsh is rewriting the Fed's own calendar, cutting a rate setting vote from 2027. Your rent, your mortgage, your grocery bill all sit downstream of this. So chat, straight answer: should the Fed have acted today?

hook.plain: The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged today with inflation still elevated. Here is what Chair Kevin Warsh said and what it means for you.
hook.mid: Rates did not move, but the Fed itself is about to change. Kevin Warsh wants fewer rate votes from 2027. Here is why that matters.
hook.bold: Inflation is still high and the Fed chose to wait. Then Warsh announced he is overhauling how the Fed sets rates. Here is what is really changing.

descs.t: A Minnesota prosecutor has charged James O'Keefe and Cam Higby with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft over an undercover video about the state's voter vouching system. Both have been summoned to court in Hennepin County. We walk through what the charges say, what the video showed, and what happens next.

James O'Keefe and Cam Higby made an undercover video of Minnesota's voter vouching system, and now Hennepin County's prosecutor has charged them with unlawful voting and identity theft. O'Keefe says it is not political but about whether citizens can still expose problems. We look at the charges, his defense, and what it means for undercover journalism.

James O'Keefe set out to show how Minnesota's voter vouching system works. Minnesota answered with felony charges of unlawful voting and identity theft against him and Cam Higby. O'Keefe says this is about whether citizens still have the right to expose fraud. Here is the case, the video at its center, and why it matters for anyone who questions how elections are run.

intro.plain: News out of Minnesota. A Hennepin County prosecutor has charged James O'Keefe and Cam Higby with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft, over their undercover video about the state's voter vouching system. Both have been summoned to court. Chat, what do you think: is this a legitimate prosecution, or going after reporters?
intro.mid: James O'Keefe made a video exposing Minnesota's voter vouching system. Now he and Cam Higby face felony charges for unlawful voting and identity theft. O'Keefe says this is not political, it is about whether citizens can still expose fraud. Chat, here is my question: where is the line between undercover journalism and breaking the law?
intro.bold: Minnesota had a choice: fix the voting loophole James O'Keefe exposed, or charge James O'Keefe. They charged him. He and Cam Higby now face felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft, and they have been summoned to court. O'Keefe says this is about your rights. Chat, be honest: would they have charged a reporter from the other side?

hook.plain: James O'Keefe and Cam Higby now face felony charges in Minnesota over an undercover voting video. Here is what they are charged with and what the video showed.
hook.mid: He filmed Minnesota's voter vouching system. Now he is charged with unlawful voting and identity theft. Here is the case against James O'Keefe, and his answer to it.
hook.bold: They exposed how Minnesota's voter vouching works, and Minnesota charged them with felonies. Here is the case against James O'Keefe and why he says it is about your rights.

descs.t: The New York Times reports that aides to Mary Peltola's campaign and Democratic operatives searched for a second Dan Sullivan to put on Alaska's Senate ballot. Reports say the Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation and Alaska's governor has ordered a probe. We walk through what the report says, what Democrats said before it, and what could happen to the ballot now.

Mary Peltola calls it a distraction, but the New York Times says her people spent months hunting for another Dan Sullivan to run against Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska. Democrats had insisted they had nothing to do with it. We look at who knew what, the reported DOJ investigation, and whether Alaska's Supreme Court could step in.

A second Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot was no accident, according to the New York Times, which reports Mary Peltola's campaign aides and Democratic operatives went looking for him. Trump wants her prosecuted, Attorney General Todd Blanche says they are cheating, and Lisa Murkowski says ballot stacking has no place in our elections. Here is the scheme, the denials, and what comes for Peltola next.

intro.plain: Big story out of Alaska. The New York Times reports aides to Mary Peltola's campaign and Democratic operatives went looking for a second Dan Sullivan to put on the Senate ballot against the real Senator Dan Sullivan. Reports say the DOJ has opened a criminal investigation, and Alaska's governor ordered one too. Chat, tell me: should a same name candidate like this stay on the ballot?
intro.mid: Mary Peltola is calling it a distraction. But the New York Times says her campaign's aides spent months finding another Dan Sullivan to run in Alaska, after Democrats insisted they had nothing to do with it. Now reports say the DOJ is investigating and Trump wants prosecutions. Chat, one question: did Peltola know, or are her staff taking the fall?
intro.bold: Democrats swore they had nothing to do with the second Dan Sullivan on Alaska's ballot. The New York Times says Peltola's own people went out and found him. Trump wants her prosecuted, the Attorney General says they are cheating, and even Lisa Murkowski is speaking out. Chat, be honest: is this the dirtiest ballot trick you have seen this cycle?

hook.plain: Two candidates named Dan Sullivan, one Senate seat. The New York Times says the second one was recruited by Mary Peltola's side. Here is what the report found and what happens next.
hook.mid: Peltola calls it a distraction. The New York Times calls it a months long search for a decoy Dan Sullivan. Here is who knew, and why the DOJ is reportedly now involved.
hook.bold: They denied it, and then the New York Times found the receipts. Peltola's people went hunting for a fake Dan Sullivan to confuse Alaska voters. Here is how the trick worked.

descs.t: Flávio Bolsonaro, the defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential runoff, has landed in Miami with his family after the US granted him entry, and says he is Brazil's rightful leader. The Washington Post reports he defied a Brazilian judicial order to surrender his passport. We walk through how he left, what his statement claims, and what Brazil's courts can do now.

Flávio Bolsonaro lost Brazil's runoff to Lula, left the country against a court order, and now says from the United States that the election was stolen and he is the true president elect. Critics say he is fleeing a criminal investigation; supporters say federal police moved on his passport seven minutes after the result. We look at both claims and what Trump's decision to let him in means.

With his father Jair Bolsonaro behind bars, Flávio Bolsonaro got out of Brazil on a private jet and landed in Miami, where he declared himself Brazil's rightful leader and vowed to lead the opposition from the US. Lula's side calls him a fugitive. Here is how he escaped, why his allies call it political persecution, and what comes next for Brazil's right.

intro.plain: Brazil now has a defeated presidential candidate claiming the presidency from Florida. Flávio Bolsonaro landed in Miami with his family after the US let him in, and the Washington Post says he defied a court order to hand over his passport. Now he says he is Brazil's rightful leader. Chat, quick question: should the US have let him in?
intro.mid: Seven minutes. That is how fast, according to Michael Shellenberger, federal police moved on Flávio Bolsonaro's passport after Brazil's result came in. Now Bolsonaro is in Miami, calling the election stolen and calling himself president. His critics call him a fugitive from a criminal investigation. Chat, which is it: persecution or escape from justice?
intro.bold: Flávio Bolsonaro is out. His father is in prison, Brazil's courts wanted his passport, and he still made it to Miami on a private jet. Now he says Brazil's election was stolen and he will lead the opposition from abroad. Lula's people call him a fugitive. Chat, tell me straight: is this persecution of Brazil's right, or a man running from the law?

hook.plain: Brazil's defeated presidential candidate is now in Miami, saying he is the country's rightful leader. Here is how he left Brazil against a court order, and what happens now.
hook.mid: Police reportedly moved on his passport seven minutes after the result. Days later, Flávio Bolsonaro was in Miami calling himself president. Here is the full chain of events.
hook.bold: His father got 27 years. Brazil's courts wanted his passport. Flávio Bolsonaro got out anyway, and now he says he is Brazil's real president. Here is how he did it.

descs.t: Donald Trump's rally in Chillicothe, Ohio was interrupted by protesters shouting that he went on Jeffrey Epstein's plane, with at least three hauled out in the first few minutes. Trump answered that he threw Epstein out of his club about 20 years ago. We walk through the footage, the hecklers and how Trump responded.

Minutes into Trump's Ohio rally, protesters started yelling about Jeffrey Epstein's plane, one after another, until security removed them. Trump's supporters call them paid protesters; one heckler posted his own footage of being pulled out. We look at what happened, what Trump said back about Epstein, and why the attack line keeps coming.

Heckler after heckler tried to derail Donald Trump's rally in Chillicothe, Ohio with Epstein taunts, and Trump fired back that he threw Jeffrey Epstein out of his club about 20 years ago. Here is the raw footage, the protesters who planned it, and how the crowd and the president handled it.

intro.plain: Trump's rally in Chillicothe, Ohio did not go to plan. Minutes in, protesters started shouting that Trump went on Jeffrey Epstein's plane, and at least three were hauled out. Trump answered that he threw Epstein out of his club about 20 years ago. Chat, what do you make of it: real protest or a stunt?
intro.mid: Five minutes. That is how long Trump's Ohio rally ran before the Epstein hecklers started, one after another, until security pulled them out. Trump's answer: he threw Jeffrey Epstein out of his club about 20 years ago. His fans say these were paid protesters. Chat, my question: does this kind of heckling help or hurt the people doing it?
intro.bold: They came to Trump's rally in Ohio with one line, Epstein's plane, and they used it one after another. Security pulled them out, and Trump hit back that he threw Epstein out of his club about 20 years ago. The crowd did not budge. Chat, be honest: did the hecklers win this one, or did Trump?

descs.t: Netanyahu's Likud party says Israel's election was stolen by Arab parties through electoral fraud and is calling on police to investigate. With 98 percent of votes counted, projections give Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 48 and Arab parties 19, with 61 needed for a majority. We walk through the numbers, Likud's claim and the paths to a government.

Neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot has the 61 seats needed to govern Israel, and the Arab parties' 19 seats now sit in the middle. Likud says the result was stolen through fraud and bribery and wants police involved, while Yair Golan urges Eisenkot's bloc to negotiate with the Arab parties. We look at the claims, the math and who can form a government.

Benjamin Netanyahu is not conceding. His Likud party says Arab parties stole Israel's election through fraud, while the opposition openly talks about relying on those same parties to push him out. With Netanyahu's bloc on 53, Eisenkot's on 48 and 61 needed, here is what Likud alleges, what the opposition is planning, and what it means for Israel's next government.

intro.plain: Israel's election has no winner yet. With 98 percent counted, projections give Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 48 and the Arab parties 19, and you need 61 to govern. Now Likud says the election was stolen through fraud by Arab parties and wants police to investigate. Chat, what do you think happens next: a deal or another election?
intro.mid: Nobody has 61. Netanyahu's bloc sits on 53, Eisenkot's on 48, and the Arab parties hold 19 seats that both sides now need to reckon with. Likud says fraud and bribery stole the result and is calling in the police. Yair Golan wants the opposition to deal with the Arab parties. Meanwhile the opposition is openly talking about a deal with those same parties to push him out. Chat, tell me straight: is this a fair fight for Israel's government or not?

descs.t: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for Ohio governor, joined Donald Trump on stage at a rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, promising the biggest property tax relief in the state and action by executive order on his first day. Senator Jon Husted also spoke. We walk through what Ramaswamy promised and how the night went.

Donald Trump flew to Chillicothe, Ohio to campaign for Vivek Ramaswamy, who pitched lower property taxes and electric bills, safer streets and better schools, plus a day one executive order. We look at his promises, the crowd's reaction, and whether the rally can move votes in the governor's race.

Vivek Ramaswamy took the stage with Donald Trump in Chillicothe, Ohio and the crowd erupted, with chants of USA through the night. He promised Ohio its biggest property tax relief and action on day one by executive order. Here is the rally, the promises and why Republicans think Ohio is theirs.

intro.plain: Trump was in Chillicothe, Ohio last night campaigning for Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor. Ramaswamy promised the biggest property tax relief in the state and action by executive order on his first day in office. Chat, question for you: what matters most to you in a governor, taxes or something else?
intro.mid: Trump flew to Ohio for one reason: get Vivek Ramaswamy elected governor.
